module

public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Erdős Problem 46

*References:*
- [erdosproblems.com/46](https://www.erdosproblems.com/46)
- [Cr03] Croot, III, Ernest S., *On a coloring conjecture about unit fractions*. Ann. of Math. (2)
  (2003), 545-556.
- [ErGr80] Erdős, P. and Graham, R., *Old and new problems and results in combinatorial number
  theory*. Monographies de L'Enseignement Mathematique (1980).
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Erdos46

/--
Does every finite colouring of the integers have a monochromatic solution to
$1=\sum \frac{1}{n_i}$ with $2\leq n_1<\cdots <n_k$?

The answer is yes, as proved by Croot [Cr03] - indeed, there are infinitely many disjoint such
monochromatic solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11, formal_proof using lean4 at "https://github.com/plby/lean-proofs/blob/main/src/v4.29.1/ErdosProblems/Erdos46.lean"]
theorem erdos_46 :
    answer(True) ↔
    -- For any finite colouring of the integers
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite →
      -- there are integers `2 ≤ n₁ < ⋯ < n_k`
      ∃ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ n ∈ S, 2 ≤ n) ∧
        -- whose reciprocals sum to `1`
        ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = 1 ∧
        -- and which all have the same colour
        (𝓒 '' (S : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

/--
Croot [Cr03] proved more: there are infinitely many disjoint such monochromatic solutions.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_46.variants.infinitely_many_disjoint :
    answer(True) ↔
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite →
      ∃ S : ℕ → Finset ℕ, (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (S i) (S j)) ∧
        ∀ i, (∀ n ∈ S i, 2 ≤ n) ∧ ∑ n ∈ S i, (1 / n : ℚ) = 1 ∧
          (𝓒 '' (S i : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

/--
In [ErGr80] they also ask for a monochromatic representation of any $\frac{a}{b}>0$.
-/
@[category research solved, AMS 5 11]
theorem erdos_46.variants.positive_rat :
    answer(True) ↔
    ∀ (𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ), (Set.range 𝓒).Finite → ∀ q : ℚ, 0 < q →
      ∃ S : Finset ℕ, (∀ n ∈ S, 2 ≤ n) ∧ ∑ n ∈ S, (1 / n : ℚ) = q ∧
        (𝓒 '' (S : Set ℕ)).Subsingleton := by
  sorry

end Erdos46

reformulations.difference: The Lean requires every denominator in the representation of q to be at least 2 (`∀ n ∈ S, 2 ≤ n`). The source's a/b question ("a monochromatic representation of any a/b>0") does not restate a lower bound on the denominators.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Requiring `2 ≤ n` is equivalent to requiring `1 ≤ n`, whatever the truth value. One direction is trivial. For the other, take the induced colouring m ↦ 𝓒(2m) and the target 2q. A representation S' of 2q with denominators ≥ 1 gives the representation S = 2·S' of q, whose denominators are ≥ 2 and which is 𝓒-monochromatic. Proved in Lean as `rat_two_iff_one`. Separately, the source's own derivation yields denominators ≥ 2b. I also derived the Lean statement from `infinitely_many_disjoint` in Lean.

reformulations.difference: The Lean asks for a sequence `S : ℕ → Finset ℕ` of pairwise disjoint solutions, each monochromatic, but different solutions may have different colours. The source's "infinitely many disjoint such monochromatic solutions" could be read as all having one colour, or as an infinite family rather than a sequence.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Each `S i` sums to 1, so it is nonempty. Pairwise disjointness then makes the `S i` distinct, so an ℕ-indexed family is exactly an infinite family of pairwise disjoint solutions. By infinite pigeonhole over the finitely many colours, infinitely many `S i` share one colour; reindexing along that fiber gives a same-colour sequence (proved in Lean as `same_colour_of_disj`). The converse is trivial.

reformulations.difference: A "finite colouring of the integers" is modelled as `𝓒 : ℕ → ℕ` with `(Set.range 𝓒).Finite`. The domain includes 0 and the colours are natural numbers, rather than a colouring of ℤ (or of the positive integers) with an abstract finite set of colours.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Solutions use only integers n ≥ 2, so the colours of 0, 1 and negative integers are irrelevant. A finite colouring of ℤ restricts to ℕ with finite range, and one of ℕ extends to ℤ (e.g. via `Int.toNat`). A finite colour set injects into ℕ. `(𝓒 '' S).Subsingleton` says exactly that S is monochromatic. I proved in Lean that the linked formal statement (`c : ℤ → α`, `[Finite α]`) implies this form. The converse direction is equally elementary but I did not formalise it.

review.notes:
No misformalizations found. All three declarations state the claims erdosproblems.com/46 poses. The answer(True) values and `research solved` tags match the source ("PROVED (LEAN)"). The module and theorem docstrings follow the page almost verbatim.

Lean evidence, all in /workspace/review:
- `(1 / n : ℚ)` elaborates to `1 / (↑n : ℚ)`.
- The parity colouring has the monochromatic solution {2,4,6,12}.
- Without the finite-range hypothesis the claim fails: the identity colouring has no solution. So the statement is neither vacuous nor trivially true.
- The linked formal theorem `Erdos46.erdos46` (plby/lean-proofs) implies the RHS of `erdos_46`. Its `rec_sum` is the same ℚ sum, and its `#print axioms` comment lists only the standard axioms.
- Sorry-free derivations (standard axioms only): RHS(`erdos_46`) ⇒ RHS(`infinitely_many_disjoint`) by recolouring each previously used integer with its own fresh colour. RHS(`infinitely_many_disjoint`) ⇒ RHS(`positive_rat`) by the source's induced-colouring argument. So all three answer(True) statements are true given the main theorem.

Minor asides, not findings:
- The `infinitely_many_disjoint` docstring says "Croot proved more". The source says "as proved by Croot – indeed, there are infinitely many disjoint such monochromatic solutions". Croot's paper states only the finite corollary, which implies the disjoint version at once.
- The formal_proof URL points at `blob/main`, not a pinned commit.
- I could not read the Erdős–Graham 1980 book (p.36) directly. `positive_rat` follows erdosproblems.com's paraphrase of it. The denominators-≥1 reading is equivalent (proved in Lean). A stronger reading, "one colour class represents every a/b", is also true (pigeonhole over b = n!), so the answer(True) stands under either reading.
